title: Good Friday
hook: churches strip altars, keep silence, and venerate the cross

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maundy Thursday: a towel, a basin, and your line: love one another. Did you do someone's least favorite job? That night ended in a garden, with an arrest. Today is the next day. Day one hundred seventeen.

Walk into a church on Good Friday, and it looks robbed. The altar is bare wood or stone. No flowers. No candles burning. The cloths are gone. In many churches, the bells don't ring. People come in without talking, and sit. Some services start at noon and run until three in the afternoon, the hours the Gospels say Jesus hung on the cross. Matthew writes: "Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." Noon to three. Christians have kept those hours for centuries, in silence, or with long readings, or with a single hymn. It's the quietest day of the Christian year. Today's word is its strange name.
screen: `A CHURCH THAT LOOKS ROBBED.` → `NO CANDLES, NO BELLS.` → `NOON TO THREE.`

segments.voice: Good Friday. First, what the Gospels say happened. After his arrest, Jesus is questioned by the high priest's council and then handed to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate sentences him, and Roman soldiers crucify him outside the city wall. Crucifixion was a Roman punishment, used for rebels and slaves, meant to be slow and public. His friends mostly scatter. Several women who had followed him from Galilee stay, watching. And in John's Gospel, his last words are three in English: "It is finished." In Greek, it's a single word, tetelestai. It doesn't mean it's over, I give up. It means it's complete. Done. Accomplished. Christians hear it as the end of a work, not a defeat. So why call the day good? Honestly, nobody is sure. Good may be the old English sense of holy. Some suggest it came from God's Friday. The sources don't settle it. But Christians call it good because they believe something was done that day for the whole world, out of love. They explain how in more than one way, and all of them look at the cross. Churches keep the day differently. Catholics celebrate no Mass; in the afternoon they read the Passion, and people come forward one by one to kneel before the cross, touch it, or kiss it. Orthodox Christians carry a cloth icon of Christ's body in procession, and lay it in a tomb covered with flowers. Many Protestants gather for three hours at noon, or for a service where candles are put out one by one, until the church is dark.
screen: `PILATE, SOLDIERS, A ROMAN CROSS.` · `TETELESTAI: IT IS COMPLETE.` · `WHY GOOD? NOBODY IS SURE.` · `THE CROSS, THE TOMB, THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep silence. Settle, and breathe. For the next two minutes, don't fill the quiet. No music, no plans, no words. If you have a cross, you can look at it. If you pray, you can simply stay near it, the way the women stayed. If you don't, let the silence be for anyone who is suffering today. Later, at noon, or whenever you can, keep three more minutes of silence. Set an alarm if you need to. The bell holds the time.
Good Friday. The day Christians remember Jesus's death on the cross, with bare altars, silence and the veneration of the cross. Today's word.
Your line: it is finished. Today, keep three minutes of silence at noon. And finish one thing you've left undone. Day one hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: On Good Friday churches are left bare and many Christians fast and keep silence; Catholics venerate the cross at an afternoon service without Mass, Orthodox Christians carry the epitaphios, an icon of Christ's burial, in procession, and many Protestants keep services from noon to three.

myth: used for rebels and slaves. Pilate, the Roman governor, sentenced Jesus.
it is finished means I give up
tetelestai means complete, accomplished. Christians hear it as a work finished, not a defeat.
the name Good Friday has one certain origin
nobody is sure: maybe good meaning holy, maybe God's Friday.

fork.setup: you're one of the women who followed Jesus from Galilee. he's on a Roman cross, and most of his friends have run. what do you do?
options: stay, and watch, and don't leave.
go and argue with the soldiers.
fork.reveal: the Gospels say several women stayed and watched. they're the ones who see where he is buried.

original.note: Greek: it is finished, completed, accomplished. one word in John 19:30.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad day with a strangely cheerful name.
what it means: the day Christians remember Jesus's death, keeping silence and honoring the cross, and hear it is finished as complete, not defeated.
what a scholar hears: tetelestai is a perfect-tense form of teleo, to bring to an end or fulfill: done, and it stays done. the name good may mean holy; its origin is uncertain.

sources.quoted: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour.

notes: Framing: Rome executes Jesus (Pilate sentences, soldiers crucify); the high priest's council questions him first. Confirm the balance is careful.
'Why good?': possible origins (good = holy/pious; 'God's Friday') presented as uncertain. Confirm.

Catholic Good Friday: Celebration of the Lord's Passion (no Mass), usually mid-afternoon, with veneration of the cross. Orthodox: epitaphios procession (often Friday evening). Protestant: Tre Ore (noon–3) and Tenebrae-style services. Confirm descriptions.
The women: Matthew 27:55–56, Mark 15:40–47 (they see where he is laid); John 19:25 places some near the cross. Confirm the fork reveal.
Atonement theories deliberately not detailed ('they explain how in more than one way'). Confirm this is acceptable across traditions.
